Subject: guess who's team lead 😊

Yash!
I had to tell you before the family group chat explodes. At 4 p.m. today my manager called me into the small meeting room and said they want me to lead the payments team from the first of next month. Me. The girl who cried over her first code review.
Five years, Yash. All those late deployments, all those weekends fixing things nobody noticed. Somebody noticed.
I called Papa from the parking lot and he didn't say anything for a few seconds, then he said, 'I'm going to tell Chachaji first.' Ma has already sent sweets to the neighbours, I'm sure. My old team took me for kulfi and Deepa made a card with a crown on it.
I keep grinning at nothing on the metro. I feel like it's been earned. Is that allowed?
Call me this weekend.
Rashmi

qa.a: From the first of next month.

qa.a: She feels proud and validated, grinning at nothing on the metro and saying it feels earned.

qa.q: What could Rashmi do to enjoy this moment and stay grounded as she starts?
qa.a: She could celebrate with the people who helped her, and keep asking her old team for honest feedback once she starts leading them.

qa.q: How might Rashmi's Papa be feeling when he goes silent for a few seconds?
qa.a: He may be overwhelmed with pride and emotion, and eager to share his daughter's news with the family.

Sunaina, sit, sit, I have to tell you properly. So at the end of the quarterly meeting, my director says, 'One more thing. From next month, Nandini will be leading the mobile team. She's earned it.' Just like that, in front of everyone. And the whole room clapped. Even Arvind, who I thought didn't like me.
I went to the washroom and just looked at myself in the mirror. Six years. You remember my first job? The one where I was fixing printers?
And then my phone went mad. My mother cried on the call, Sunaina. My brother sent twenty messages in capitals. Your mother even messaged me! How did she know so fast?
I know it's just a title. But it doesn't feel like just a title. It feels like someone finally looked at all those years and said yes, we saw.
Okay, stop smiling at me. Order the samosas, I'm paying.

qa.a: The whole room clapped, even Arvind.

qa.a: She feels her long effort has been seen and rewarded, and that the promotion validates her.

qa.a: She could keep meeting old friends like Sunaina and colleagues like Arvind the same way, so the glow doesn't change how she treats people.

qa.a: Sunaina gets to share a friend's joy up close and is clearly happy for Nandini, since Nandini tells her to stop smiling.

Tuesday. The director called Akash into the glass room and said the words he had waited four years for: "We'd like you to lead the payments team." He walked out trying to look calm and went straight to the stairwell to call his mother. She cried on the phone. So did he, a little.
Friday. His old college friend Saurabh booked a table at the Andhra place they used to go to as interns. The whole team came, clapping as he walked in. Someone had printed "Lead Engineer Akash" on a paper crown. He wore it all evening.
Sunday. At home, his father, who never said much, told the neighbours at the gate, "My son is managing people now." Akash overheard from the balcony and felt something warm settle in his chest. After all the late nights, it felt earned. Fair. His.

qa.a: Lead Engineer Akash.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when he overheard his father on Sunday?
qa.a: He felt proud and validated, a warm sense that the promotion was a fair reward for years of effort.

qa.q: What could Akash do in this glow to prepare well for the new role?
qa.a: Enjoy the moment, and also ask his old teammates what they need from a lead before the real work begins.

qa.a: Saurabh is happy and proud for an old friend, remembering their intern days at the same restaurant.

passage:
Rafiq, you look exactly like I did the day they made me shift supervisor at the textile mill in Coimbatore. I was twenty-five. Pallavi, the first woman supervisor on that floor in thirty years.
The manager read my name at the morning meeting, and the women from my old line started clapping before he finished. I had worked seven years on those looms. Seven years of double shifts. That evening my mother made payasam and sent some to every house on our street. My father, who had never once asked about my work, put on his good shirt and walked me to the bus the next morning.
I felt I had climbed a hill with my own hands. And I had. I let myself feel that fully.
But that same week I had to choose how I would treat the women I'd worked beside. That choice is the rest of the story, and you are about to face it too.

qa.q: How many years had Pallavi worked on the looms?
qa.a: Seven years.

qa.q: How did young Pallavi feel when her name was read out?
qa.a: She felt proud and validated, as if she had climbed a hill with her own hands after seven years.

qa.q: What choice in the story does Pallavi point to as the turning point?
qa.a: How she would treat the women she had worked beside, a choice that came in the same week as the promotion.

qa.q: What did the promotion mean to Pallavi's father in the story?
qa.a: He seemed quietly proud, putting on his good shirt and walking her to the bus, though he had never asked about her work.

grounding: An elder recalls being promoted to supervisor after years of hard work, feeling proud and validated as her family celebrated.

The email arrived while Himani was stuck at Itarsi junction, her train to Delhi seven hours late, phone at eleven per cent, the platform crowded with people asleep on bedrolls. Subject line: Promotion to Team Lead, Backend.
She read it three times. Four years of fixing other people's code at midnight, and someone had noticed. She wanted to shout, but the man on the bench beside her was asleep with his mouth open.
She had battery for exactly one call. Not her manager, not the team chat. She called Sonali.
"I'm a team lead," she whispered.
Sonali screamed so loudly that the sleeping man woke up. "I knew it! I told you they'd see it!"
Himani laughed and cried at the same time, and a chaiwala who had overheard handed her a free cup. "For the new boss," he said.
Her phone died two minutes later. She didn't mind at all.

qa.q: Where was Himani stuck when the email arrived?
qa.a: At Itarsi junction, her train to Delhi seven hours late.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling as she read the email three times?
qa.a: She felt proud and validated, thrilled that four years of midnight fixes had finally been noticed.

qa.q: What could Himani do once she is home to carry this glow wisely into the role?
qa.a: Celebrate with family, then thank the team she worked with and ask what they hope for from a new lead.

qa.q: What is the moment like for Sonali on the phone?
qa.a: Sonali is overjoyed and a little vindicated, having long believed Himani's work would be recognised.

grounding: Stuck on a delayed journey with a dying phone, a young engineer learns she is team lead and feels proud and validated as a friend celebrates.

At dinner Appa told the whole family, twice, "She earned it." Lying awake that night, Nirmala thought: yes, I did.
